title: Do not kill
hook: Jesus deepens it to anger and contempt (Matthew 5:22)

segments.voice: Yesterday, honor your parents: give the old their weight. Your line was honor the old. Who did you call, or sit with? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

"Thou shalt not kill." On paper it can sound like the easiest commandment on the list. Get through the day without killing anyone, and you're finished. Then Jesus sees the crowds, goes up a mountain and sits down, his disciples come to him, and he moves the line. Not just the knife. The anger. Not just the act. The word you call your brother. Today: do not kill, and how far into the heart it reaches.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says: "Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill." Then he goes further. "But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment." He goes on to an insult, Raca, which the King James leaves untranslated, and then to "Thou fool." He isn't saying anger and murder are the same thing. He's tracing murder back to its root. Before a hand ever moves, a heart decides that someone doesn't count. Contempt is the seed: a fool, a nobody, a waste of space. That's the word that makes harm thinkable. Then he turns practical. If you're about to worship and remember that someone has something against you: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." Repair comes before ritual. Some translations render the commandment you shall not murder, reading it as unlawful killing. Christians disagree, seriously and in good faith, about war, self-defense and the death penalty. Mennonite and Quaker traditions teach nonviolence. Other churches teach that force can sometimes be just. Jesus's reading puts all of them in front of the same test, closer to home than any battlefield: the contempt we let ourselves say.

Here's the practice: catch contempt before it speaks. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've quietly written off: a coworker, a relative, a public figure, a driver from this morning. Notice the word you use for them in your head. Idiot. Useless. Hold that word up and look at it. Then try calling them what Jesus does: a brother, a sister. You don't have to like them. Just set the word down. If you pray, you can pray for them, using their name instead of the word. The bell holds the time.
Do not kill. The commandment against taking life, which Jesus traces back to anger and contempt in the heart.
Your line: not even in the heart. Today, when a contemptuous word rises about someone, catch it before you say it or type it. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians read this commandment alongside the Sermon on the Mount, so preaching on it often turns to anger, insult and reconciliation; churches differ on war and the death penalty, with Mennonites and Quakers holding to nonviolence and others teaching just-war principles.

Editor pass: hook said the insult is used 'once they've left the room', but Matthew 5:22 is about what one says to one's brother; hook and screen now say 'the word you call your brother'. Unsourced claims removed: 'Raca, a word nobody can translate with certainty' (now: the King James leaves it untranslated) and 'the Hebrew verb is usually understood as murder' (now: some translations say murder), in teach, match and trapdoor. 'Mennonites and Quakers hold to' became 'Mennonite and Quaker traditions teach'. Carry's 'mouth or thumbs' changed to avoid repeating day 1186.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): hook said Jesus sat 'with the crowd around him'; Matthew 5:1 has him see the crowds, go up and sit, and his disciples come to him, so the hook now follows the text. Practice's prayer line varied (it repeated day 1187's 'name them before God').
